question: How can an attention-only transformer infer which lag generated a sequence, estimate the corresponding transition rule in context, and select the right induction circuit rather than applying a fixed copying rule?

key_findings.claim: A three-layer attention circuit can implement lag-conditioned next-token prediction on interleaved Markov chains.
key_findings.evidence: The construction's first layer forms empirical transition probabilities for candidate lags, the second aggregates non-overlapping evidence over the history, and the third uses a low-temperature selective induction head to copy from the lag with the largest aggregated normalized score.

anchors.section: 5 How can transformers do in-context selection? / Proposition 1

key_findings.claim: The estimator approaches maximum-likelihood lag selection only asymptotically and under a restricted synthetic generative model.
key_findings.evidence: The analysis assumes candidate sources share one irreducible aperiodic transition matrix and differ only by lag. The proof compares expected normalized transition scores as sequence length grows; finite-context Bayesian model averaging is not exactly implemented, and the strongest convergence statements require conditions detailed around Proposition 1 and the appendix.

anchors.section: Bayesian model average and MLE limit

key_findings.claim: Gradient-trained standard and disentangled transformers recover behavior and attention patterns close to the hand construction on the tested lag sets.
key_findings.evidence: Across contiguous, non-contiguous, and two-lag tasks, trained three-layer models reach the constructed estimator and maximum-likelihood curves. Their first two layers exhibit transition-extraction and aggregation patterns, while the last layer selects the inferred lag. Adding second-layer heads helps until the number of candidate lags, after which performance saturates.

key_findings.claim: The evidence identifies a mechanism for the designed task, not yet a causal-structure selector in natural-language models.
key_findings.evidence: Every experiment trains small attention-only models from scratch on finite-alphabet Markov sequences. There is no intervention on a pretrained language model, natural-language evaluation, or demonstration that a visually similar head is necessary and sufficient outside the synthetic distribution.

anchors.section: 4 Markov chains and causal structure selection

method.core_idea: Use interleaved Markov chains with identical transition probabilities but different lags to isolate in-context selection of a causal dependency.
method.mechanism: Construct and train three-layer attention-only transformers whose layers estimate lag-specific transitions, aggregate evidence, and sharply attend to the parent token implied by the winning lag.
assumptions: Candidate lag set is known during training.
All sources share a stationary irreducible aperiodic transition matrix.
Long sequences make the normalized score identify the generating lag.
The disentangled attention construction can be related to a standard attention-only transformer.

techniques.role: Varies causal lag while holding token-transition semantics fixed.
Assigns transition extraction, evidence aggregation, and lag selection to separate attention layers.
Ranks candidate lags using accumulated empirical transition compatibility.
Compares trained heads with the explicit algorithmic circuit.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic sequences over sampled transition matrices with candidate lag sets {1,2,3}, {1,3,4}, larger contiguous sets, and {1,3}.
evaluations.metric: Next-token loss/performance relative to maximum likelihood and Bayesian model averaging.
evaluations.result: Constructed and trained three-layer transformers approach the maximum-likelihood estimator on the tested settings.
evaluations.baseline: Maximum-likelihood estimator, Bayesian model average, and under-provisioned transformer variants.

evaluations.setting: Three-layer standard and disentangled attention-only transformers trained from scratch.
evaluations.result: Maps qualitatively reproduce transition extraction, diagonal aggregation, and final lag-selective attention.

evaluations.setting: Five-lag task with varying second-layer head count.
evaluations.metric: Predictive performance as heads are added.
evaluations.result: Performance improves up to approximately one aggregation head per lag and then does not improve beyond the maximum-likelihood ceiling.
evaluations.baseline: Models with fewer or more heads than candidate lags.

limitations: Author scope: the task is a simplified finite-state proxy rather than natural language.
Reviewer inference: candidate structures differ only by lag and share one transition matrix, excluding structure-semantic confounding.
Reviewer inference: attention-map similarity does not establish causal necessity without ablation or activation-level intervention.
Reviewer inference: asymptotic score separation leaves finite-context sample complexity only partially characterized.
failure_modes: Two candidate lags induce nearly indistinguishable finite-sample score distributions.
Nonstationarity or lag-dependent transition matrices make the normalized score confound structure with semantics.
Too few aggregation heads lose transition evidence; short contexts do not concentrate on the true lag.
A trained model solves the task with a distributed representation that is not captured by the hand circuit.
reusable_insights: Varying structure while holding local transition statistics fixed is a clean way to test contextual rule selection.
An interpretable circuit claim is stronger when an explicit construction, trained-model behavior, and controlled head-count ablation agree.
Model selection in context can be decomposed into candidate estimation, global evidence accumulation, and conditional execution.
open_questions: Do pretrained language models contain causally necessary selective induction heads for ambiguous natural-language dependencies?
What is the finite-sequence error rate as a function of lag separation, alphabet size, mixing time, and number of candidates?
Can one circuit select richer graph or latent-state structures rather than a single lag?
How robust is the learned selector when the test lag was unseen during training?

competitive_landscape.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
competitive_landscape.difference: Olsson et al. connect ordinary previous-token induction heads to in-context learning; this paper makes the copied offset itself context-dependent through an evidence-aggregation circuit.

competitive_landscape.title: How Transformers Learn Causal Structure with Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Nichani et al. analyze recovery of a fixed Markov causal graph and its transition probabilities; this work requires selecting among several lag structures within each context.

competitive_landscape.title: The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads: In-Context Learning Markov Chains
competitive_landscape.difference: Edelman et al. study statistical induction for bigram posterior prediction, whereas selective induction first compares multiple causal lags and then executes the inferred one.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformers as Statisticians: Provable In-Context Learning with In-Context Algorithm Selection
competitive_landscape.difference: Bai et al. prove selection among regression/classification algorithms from demonstrations; this paper isolates causal-lag selection and supplies a mechanistic attention circuit.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper introduces selective induction heads and constructs a three-layer transformer that selects a causal lag in context and asymptotically implements maximum-likelihood prediction.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Proposition 1, the statistical score analysis, trained-versus-constructed performance, and attention-map comparisons support the claim within the interleaved-Markov setting.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The meaningful novelty is a mechanistically explicit model-selection circuit, but generalization from lag selection to natural-language causal structure remains an untested hypothesis.
